concept.name: Event risk
concept.definition: The risk that a discrete, often unforecastable event — a takeover, reorganization, credit downgrade, product recall, regulatory action, natural disaster, or overnight headline — abruptly reprices a security or portfolio, independent of the prevailing market trend.
concept.intuition: You can be right about the market and still get wiped out by the press release: event risk is the discrete shock that doesn't care about your chart.
concept.mechanics: Events reprice securities by jump rather than continuous path, so protection uses insurance-like instruments (options, credit default swaps), event-driven exposure cuts (flat before earnings), and stop orders — which only partially help because event moves often gap. In credit markets, event risk includes sudden downgrades that raise issuers' funding costs.
concept.formula: No canonical formula; exposure is scenario-based: P/L impact = position sensitivity * event-induced price jump.
concept.failure_modes: The events that matter are the ones not on the calendar — unscheduled shocks cannot be sidestepped with an earnings-date filter — and hedges carry carry costs and counterparty considerations of their own. Stop orders give limited protection because event moves gap through them.
concept.misconceptions: Event risk is not just volatility around scheduled news — its defining cases are unforeseen — and holding many names in one event-prone sector (e.g. biotech trial readouts) does not diversify the shared event factor.
concept.example: A merger-arbitrage position in a takeover target loses heavily when regulators unexpectedly block the deal; the spread gaps wider overnight with no chance to exit at yesterday's price.
